ÖOptimal Algorithm for 2-Approximate All Pair Shortest Paths -- almost **Abstract** Given an undirected, unweighted graph G, we aim to compute a 2-approximation of all-pairs shortest paths (APSP). This problem admits a natural lower bound of \(\Omega(n^2)\) since the output size is \(\Theta(n^2)\). A central goal in this area is to achieve a running time of O(n2). Dor, Halperin, and Zwick (FOCS 1996, SICOMP 2001) designed an algorithm with a running time1 of \(\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^2)\) that guarantees a 2-approximation only for pairs at a distance of at least O(logn). Recently, Gupta (FOCS 2025) improved this bound, handling all pairs at a distance of at least O(loglogn). We nearly resolve this problem. We design a randomized algorithm that runs in \(\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^2)\) time and, with high probability2, guarantees a 2-approximation for all pairs at distance at least c, where \(c\ge 0\) is a constant. Unlike the above two results, which were purely combinatorial, our algorithm combines combinatorial techniques with fast matrix multiplication (FMM). ## 1 Introduction Let G=(V,E) be an unweighted, undirected graph with n vertices and m edges. Let st denote a shortest path between vertices s and t in G, and let |st| denote its length. Computing all pairs shortest paths in a graph G is a fundamental problem in graph algorithms. For unweighted graphs, a simple combinatorial algorithm computes all pairs shortest paths in O(mn) time. Seidel [Sei95] designed an algorithm that uses fast matrix multiplication (FMM) and solved the problem in \(\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^\omega)\) time, where \(n^\omega\) denotes the time required to multiply two \(n\times n\) matrices. Even with the advancements in fast matrix multiplication in [AW24, Gal14, Sto10, Wil12, DWZ23, WXXZ24], this running time remains superquadratic. To achieve near quadratic running time, we must allow approximate solutions. Let est(s,t) denote the estimate of the shortest path between s and t returned by an algorithm. We say that the algorithm is \((\alpha,\beta)\) approximate, for \(\alpha\ge 1\) and \(\beta\ge 0\), if \(|\mathrm{st}|\le\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{s},\mathrm{t})\le\alpha|\mathrm{st}|+\beta,\text{for all}\mathrm{s},\mathrm{t}\text{pairs in}\mathrm{G}\) If \(\beta=0\), we obtain a purely multiplicative approximation and call the algorithm an \(\alpha\) approximate all pairs shortest paths algorithm, or \(\alpha\)-APSP algorithm in short. If \(\alpha=1\), we obtain a purely additive approximation and call the algorithm a +\(\beta\)-APSP algorithm. <tbc>Dor, Halperin and Zwick \[DHZ00\] showed that obtaining \((2-\varepsilon)\)-APSP is as hard as Boolean Matrix Multiplication. Consequently, obtaining a nearly quadratic algorithm for \(\alpha\)-APSP with \(\alpha<2\) would imply a major breakthrough in matrix multiplication (i.e., \(\omega=2\)). But what about the case when \(\alpha=2\) or 2-APSP? The only natural lower bound is the output size, which is \(\Theta(n^2)\). Thus, any 2-APSP algorithm requires \(\Omega(n^2)\) time. Since no stronger lower bound is known, an important problem is to design a 2-APSP algorithm that runs in O(n<sup>2</sup>) time.

We will see later that purely additive APSP algorithms are used to obtain 2-APSP. We now describe results for purely additive APSP. Aingworth, Chekuri, Indyk and Motwani \[ACIM99\] designed a \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2.5})\) time algorithm for +2-APSP. Later, Dor, Halperin and Zwick \[DHZ00\] reduced the running time to \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{min}\{n^{3/2}m^{1/2},n^{7/3}\})\). Using FMM, Deng, Kirkpatrick, Rong, Williams and Zhong \[DKR<sup>+</sup>22\] improved the running time to O(n<sup>2.259</sup>) (using an improved result of \[Dür23\]). Very recently, Jin, Kirkpatrick, Stawarz and Williams \[JKSV26\], again using FMM, improved this running time to O(n<sup>2.2255</sup>).

We now describe a simple relation that yields a 2-APSP from a purely additive approximation.

**Observation 1.1.** _A_ +k-APSP _implies a_ 2-APSP _for all pairs of vertices at distance at least_ k.

Since we can find a path of length one in O(m) time, the above observation translates the +2-APSP from the previous paragraph to 2-APSP. However, all these algorithms require \(\omega(n^2)\) time. Fortunately, there are +k-APSP algorithms with better running times. Dor, Halperin and Zwick \[DHZ00\] designed a +k-APSP algorithm with running time \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{min}\{n^{2-\frac{2}{k+2}}m^\frac{2}{k+2},n^{2+\frac{2}{3k-2}}\})\). Saha and Ye \[SY24\] recently used FMM to improve the running time. However, the worst case running time in these results remain \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2+\mathrm{O}(\frac{1}{k})})\). If k=logn, then the running time becomes \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) and the algorithm works for all pairs of vertices at a distance at least O(logn). Until recently, this was the best result for 2-APSP with the running time \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\).

Gupta \[Gup25\] designed an algorithm for 2-APSP that runs in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2+1/k})\) time and works for vertices at distance at least O(logk). If k=logn, then the running time becomes \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\), and the algorithm works for all pairs at a distance at least O(loglogn). An important open problem in this field is to design a 2-APSP algorithm that works for all pairs and runs in O(n<sup>2</sup>) time or nearly optimal \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) time. We nearly resolve this problem by showing the following theorem.

**Theorem 1.2.** _There exists a randomized algorithm that, with high probability, runs in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) _time and computes_ 2-APSP _for all pairs of vertices at distance at least_ c_, where_ \(\mathrm{c}\unknown 0\) _is a constant._

We do not attempt to optimize the constant, though we achieve \(\mathrm{c}\unknown 906\). Our approach builds on the combinatorial techniques developed by Gupta \[Gup25\]. Our algorithm also builds some combinatorial techniques but a crucial step of our algorithm uses FMM. The primary contribution of our work is showing how to combine these combinatorial techniques with FMM.

## 1.1 Other related results

There is another class of algorithms that do not use Theorem 1.1 and compute 2-APSP directly. These algorithms work for all pairs of vertices. Cohen and Zwick \[CZ01\] designed an \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{3/2}m^{1/2})\) time algorithm for 2-APSP. Baswana and Kavitha \[BK06\] achieved a running time of \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(m\sqrt{n}+n^2)\). Roditty \[Rod23\] designed a combinatorial algorithm for 2-APSP in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2.25})\) time. All of the above algorithms are combinatorial in nature. Using FMM, Dory, Forster, Kirkpatrick, Nazari, Williams, and Vos \[DFK<sup>+</sup>24\] and Saha and Ye \[SY24\] improved the running time to \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2.031})\). There are many combinatorial algorithms \[BK07, Som16, Knu17, PR10\] that compute a (2,1)-APSP in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) time.

### Weighted graphs

The algorithms of \[CZ01, BK06\] work for weighted graphs. The authors \[CZ01, BK06\] also designed a 3-APSP algorithm that runs in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) time. Kavitha \[Kav12\] designed a \((2+\varepsilon)\)-APSP algorithm for<tbc>

<tbc>weighted graphs running in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2.25})\) time. Baswana and Kavitha \[BK06\] designed an algorithm that computes a (2_,W_<sub>s,t</sub>)-APSP in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) time, where _W_<sub>s,t</sub> is the maximum edge weight on the shortest path between s and t.

## 2 Overview

Using Theorem 1.1, a +O(1)-APSP implies a 2-approximation for all pairs at a constant distance from each other. In the overview, we describe the intuition behind an algorithm that provides a constant additive approximation for the shortest path between s and t. However, our algorithm relies on certain structural assumptions that do not hold in general. We first introduce the notation used in this overview and throughout the paper.

### 2.1 Basic notations

**Definition 2.1** (Estimate between a pair of vertices)**.** _For every pair_ (s,t) _we maintain_ est(s,t)_, which is our current best estimate of the length of the_ st _path. Several known algorithms compute_ (2,1)_-approximate all-pairs shortest paths in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) _time \[BK07, Som16, Knu17, PR10\]. We therefore assume that_ \(|\mathrm{st}|\le\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{s},\mathrm{t})\le 2|\mathrm{st}|+1\) _is maintained throughout the algorithm. Whenever we update_ est(s,t)_, we also update_ est(t,s).

Let A be a set of vertices obtained by sampling each vertex of V independently with probability \(\frac{1}{n^{0.05}}\). Hence, with high probability, \(|A|=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{0.95})\). The exponent 0.05 does not play any special role in the analysis. Any sufficiently small constant exponent would suffice for our purposes. We now introduce some additional notations.

**Definition 2.2** (Pivots, Balls and Clusters)**.** _For each_ \(\mathrm{s}\in\mathrm{V}\)_, let_ pivot<sub>A</sub>(s) _denote the vertex in_ A _closest to_ s _in_ G_, breaking ties arbitrarily. Let_ ball<sub>A</sub>(s) _be the set of vertices strictly closer to_ s _than_ pivot<sub>A</sub>(s)_. Formally,_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{s})=\{\mathrm{v}||\mathrm{sv}|<|\mathrm{spivot}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{s})|\}\)

<tbc>_For each_ \(\mathrm{v}\in\mathrm{V}\)_, let_ cluster<sub>A</sub>(v) _be the set of vertices whose ball contains_ v_. Formally,_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{cluster}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{v})=\{\mathrm{s}|\mathrm{v}\in\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{s})\}\)

<tbc>Balls and clusters are well known concepts in the literature on approximate shortest paths. One can show that \(|\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{s})|=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{0.05})\) with high probability. However, \(|\mathrm{cluster}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{v})|\) may be large.<tbc>

Thorup and Zwick \[TZ01\] presented a sampling method that bounds the size of clusters as well. For the overview, we assume the following.

**Assumption 2.3.** _For each_ \(s\in\mathsf{V}\), \(|\mathsf{ball}_A(s)|=\tilde{\mathsf{O}}(\mathsf{n}^{0.05})\) _and_ \(|\mathsf{cluster}_A(s)|=\tilde{\mathsf{O}}(\mathsf{n}^{0.05})\).

Observe that the ball contains all vertices at distance \(\le|\mathsf{s}\mathsf{pivot}_A(s)|-1\) from s. No vertex strictly inside the ball, that is, at distance \(\le|\mathsf{s}\mathsf{pivot}_A(s)|-2\) from s, has degree greater than \(\tilde{\mathsf{O}}(\mathsf{n}^{0.05})\), since otherwise the ball size exceeds \(\tilde{\mathsf{O}}(\mathsf{n}^{0.05})\). Thus, we obtain the following lemma.

**Lemma 2.4.** _For each_ \(s\in\mathsf{V}\)_, every vertex strictly inside_ ball<sub>A</sub>(s)_, that is, at distance_ \(\le|\mathsf{s}\mathsf{pivot}_A(s)|-2\) _from s, has degree_ \(\le\tilde{\mathsf{O}}(\mathsf{n}^{0.05})\).

## 2.2 A new idea

We now present a new approach to this problem. To connect the local balls of s and t to the global shortest path, we examine where the st path crosses the boundaries of their respective balls.

**Definition 2.5.** _Assuming_ \(t\notin\mathsf{ball}_A(s)\) _and_ \(s\notin\mathsf{ball}_A(t)\)_, let_ p<sub>s</sub> _denote the vertex on the boundary of_ ball<sub>A</sub>(s) _that lies on the_ st _path. Similarly, let_ p<sub>t</sub> _denote the vertex on the boundary of_ ball<sub>A</sub>(t) _that lies on the_ st _path. See Figure 1. Thus_ |sp<sub>s</sub>|=|spivot<sub>A</sub>(s)|-1 _and_ |tp<sub>t</sub>|=|tpivot<sub>A</sub>(t)|-1.

Using Theorem 2.4, each vertex on the sp<sub>s</sub> path, except possibly p<sub>s</sub>, has degree \(\le\tilde{\mathsf{O}}(\mathsf{n}^{0.05})\). We make the same argument for the vertices on the p<sub>t</sub>t path. Thus, the prefix sp<sub>s</sub> and the suffix p<sub>t</sub>t of the st path have low degree, and we will use this crucially to design faster algorithms. But what about the middle segment, p<sub>s</sub>p<sub>t</sub>? Unfortunately, p<sub>s</sub>p<sub>t</sub> may contain vertices with high degree. But what if we could show that p<sub>s</sub>p<sub>t</sub> is short? This is exactly our main assumption in this section.

**Assumption 2.6.** \(|\mathsf{p}_\mathsf{s}\mathsf{p}_\mathsf{t}|\le\mathsf{c}\)_, where_ c _is a constant._

We will prove this assumption in later sections. But how does it help us find the st path? By definition, \(s\in\mathsf{cluster}_A(\mathsf{p}_\mathsf{s})\) and \(t\in\mathsf{cluster}_A(\mathsf{p}_\mathsf{t})\). Unfortunately, given s and t, we do not know the identities of p<sub>s</sub> and p<sub>t</sub>. But what if we just guess them? Consider the following simple algorithm that iterates over all pairs x and y, treating them as candidates for p<sub>s</sub> and p<sub>t</sub>, and checks the paths between their clusters.

Since the algorithm checks all candidate pairs x and y, it will eventually process the specific iteration where x=ps and y=pt. Consider this specific pair (ps,pt). Because our algorithm takes the minimum over all pairs, checking the specific pair (ps,pt) gives us an upper bound on est(s,t): \(\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{s},\mathrm{t})\le\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{s},\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s},\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t})+\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t},\mathrm{t})\) Later in our paper, we will show that we can find the exact distance between s and all the vertices in ballA(s) quickly. Thus, est(s,ps)=|sps|. Similarly, est(t,pt)=|ptt|. Thus, we get: \(=|\mathrm{sp}_\mathrm{s}|+\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s},\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t})+|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}\mathrm{t}|\) By Theorem 2.1, \(\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s},\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t})\le 2|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}|+1\). Thus, we get: \(\le|\mathrm{sp}_\mathrm{s}|+(2|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}|+1)+|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}\mathrm{t}|\)
\(=(|\mathrm{sp}_\mathrm{s}|+|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}|+|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}\mathrm{t}|)+|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}|+1\) Since ps and pt lie exactly on the shortest st path, |sps|+|pspt|+|ptt|=|st|. Using Theorem 2.6, \(|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}|\le\mathrm{c}\). Thus, we get: \(\le|\mathrm{st}|+\mathrm{c}+1\) (1) Thus, we get a constant additive approximation of the st path. Let us now look at the running time of our algorithm. Using Theorem 2.3, |clusterA(x)|,|clusterA(y)|=\(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{n}^{0.05})\). Thus, the running time of our algorithm is bounded by: \(\sum_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{y}}\sum_{\mathrm{s}\in\mathrm{cluster}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{x}),\mathrm{t}\in\mathrm{cluster}_\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{y})}\mathrm{O}(1)=\sum_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{y}}\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{n}^{0.05}\times\mathrm{n}^{0.05})=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{n}^{2.1})\) Algorithm 1 processes all pairs x and y, resulting in an undesirable \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{n}^{2.1})\) running time. But do we really need to check all pairs? By Theorem 2.6, we know that our target vertices ps and pt are at most a distance c apart. Unfortunately, our current algorithm blindly pairs vertices that are arbitrarily far from each other. But what if, for a given x, we only check candidates y that are close to it? We define the following set to restrict our search space. **Definition 2.7.** _For each_ \(\mathrm{x}\in\mathrm{V}\)_, we compute a set_ ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x) _defined as follows:_ \(\mathrm{ESTIMATEDCLOSE}(\mathrm{x})=\{\mathrm{y}|\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{x},\mathrm{y})\le 2\mathrm{c}+1\}\) Using Theorem 2.6, \(|\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s}\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t}|\le\mathrm{c}\). Since we have pre-calculated a (2,1)-APSP, \(\mathrm{est}(\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{s},\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{t})\le 2\mathrm{c}+1\). Thus, ESTIMATEDCLOSE(ps) contains pt. We now modify Algorithm 1: instead of pairing x with every vertex in the graph, we pair it only with vertices in ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x). This modification improves the running time when ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x) is small. Unfortunately, if |ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x)|=O(n), then the algorithm still performs as poorly as Algorithm 1. But what if we use the size of ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x) to our advantage? We now present our final insight. For each candidate vertex x, we divide the algorithm into two cases based on size of ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x): 1. **Sparse Case:** \(|\mathrm{ESTIMATEDCLOSE}(\mathrm{x})|\le\mathrm{n}^{0.875}\) In this case, we use a modified version of Algorithm 1. We only pair x with vertices \(\mathrm{y}\in\mathrm{ESTIMATEDCLOSE}(\mathrm{x})\). Since the size of ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x) is bounded, the number of pairs processed for a given x reduces to O(n0.875). Across all sparse vertices, this takes time:

\(\sum_x\sum_{y\in\text{ESTIMATEDCLOSE}(x)}\sum_{s\in\text{cluster}_A(x),t\in\text{cluster}_A(y)}\text{O}(1)\)
\(=\sum_x\sum_{y\in\text{ESTIMATEDCLOSE}(x)}\tilde{\text{O}}(n^{0.05}\times n^{0.05})\)
\(=\sum_x\tilde{\text{O}}(n^{0.875}\times n^{0.1})\)
\(=\tilde{\text{O}}(n^{1.975})\) Thus, the running time of our algorithm is less than \(\tilde{\text{O}}(n^2)\). We now move to the second case. 2. **Dense Case:** |ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x)|_\>_n0.875 In this case, we exploit the fact that ESTIMATEDCLOSE(x) is large. Let L be a set of vertices sampled from V with probability \(\tilde{\text{O}}\left(\frac{1}{n^{0.875}}\right)\). With high probability, \(|\text{L}|=\tilde{\text{O}}(n^{0.125})\), meaning L is a very small set. Moreover, with high probability, L contains at least one vertex \(z\in\text{ESTIMATEDCLOSE}(x)\). We therefore estimate the distance using the vertices of L as intermediaries: \(est(s,t)=min_{z\in\text{L}}\{est(s,z)+est(z,t)\}\) Later, we show that est(s,t) is a constant additive approximation of |st| and that we can compute these estimates concurrently for all dense vertices using Fast Matrix Multiplication (FMM). Because \(|\text{L}|=\tilde{\text{O}}(n^{0.125})\), this computation involves multiplying small rectangular matrices of size \(n\times n^{0.125}\) and \(n^{0.125}\times n\). Following \[Cop82, Wil14\], we can multiply these matrices in \(\tilde{\text{O}}(n^2)\) time. Thus, the running time of our algorithm remains \(\tilde{\text{O}}(n^2)\) despite the use of FMM. Because the algorithm correctly handles every candidate x, it successfully approximates the st path when it processes x=ps. If ESTIMATEDCLOSE(ps) is sparse, the modified algorithm checks the pair (ps,pt) and computes an additive approximation of the st path. If ESTIMATEDCLOSE(ps) is dense, one of the vertices in the random set L lies near the st path, and the FMM step guarantees we find a good approximation. To summarise, the key takeaway from this overview is the following. The st path naturally decomposes into three segments: the low-degree prefix sps, the short middle segment pspt, and the low- degree suffix ptt. The prefix and suffix are handled cheaply because their low-degree structure allows efficient exact distance computation inside balls. The middle segment is handled by the sparse/dense case split: if few vertices are close to ps, we enumerate them directly; if many are, a small random sample is guaranteed to hit one, and FMM does the rest. The entire approach hinges on Theorem 2.6, which ensures the middle segment is short. Justifying this assumption is the main technical contribution of the subsequent sections, and we use the recent work of Gupta \[Gup25\] to establish it. ## 3 Preliminaries Let G be an undirected unweighted graph with n vertices and m edges. Let V and E denote the vertex and edge sets of G. For any pair s,t, let st denote a shortest path between s and t. If multiple shortest paths exist, pick one arbitrarily. Let |st| denote the length of st. Let deg(s) denote the degree of a vertex \(s\in V\). We denote an edge between two adjacent vertices s and t by (s,t). For brevity, we will assume that log log n is an integer.

Although our problem is defined on an unweighted graph, our algorithm constructs several auxiliary graphs that may contain weighted edges. We denote a weighted edge from s to t in such graphs by \[s,t\] and denote its weight by \(|[s,t]|\). The degree of an edge _e_=(s,t) is deg(_e_):=min{deg(_s),_deg(t)}. For two paths P and Q where P ends at the vertex where Q starts, we denote by \(P\odot Q\) the concatenation of P and Q.

Baswana and Kavitha \[BK06\] proposed an \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(m\sqrt{n}+n^2)\) time algorithm for 2-APSP. We can use this result to find 2-approximate shortest paths for pairs connected entirely by low-degree vertices (degree at most \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{n})\)). To achieve this, we construct a subgraph H of G containing only vertices with degree at most \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{n})\). Note that all low-degree paths from G are preserved in H. Since the maximum degree in H is \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{n})\), the number of edges in H is at most \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n\sqrt{n})\). Applying the algorithm from \[BK06\] to H takes \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) overall time. We therefore assume the following for the rest of the paper.

**Assumption 3.1.** _The shortest_ st _path contains at least one vertex with degree_ \(\ge\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{n})\).

In our paper we use the algorithm of Gupta \[Gup25\]. We now introduce some notations from it.

**Definition 3.2** (Nested Vertex Sampling)**.** _Let_ A<sub>0</sub>=V_. Let_ A<sub>1</sub> _be the set of vertices sampled from_ A<sub>0</sub> _with probability_ \(\frac{1}{2^{2^\mathrm{i}}}\)_. For each_ \(2\le\mathrm{i}\le\mathrm{loglog}n-1\), A<sub>i</sub> _is sampled from_ A<sub>i-1</sub> _with probability_ \(\frac{1}{2^{2^{\mathrm{i}-1}}}\).

One can show that \(|A_\mathrm{i}|=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{n}{2^{2^\mathrm{i}}})\) with high probability. We now move on to the other notations used in \[Gup25\].

**Definition 3.3** (Pivots, Balls and Clusters)**.** _For each_ \(s\in\mathsf{V}\)_, let_ pivot<sub>i</sub>(s) _denote the vertex in_ A<sub>i</sub> _closest to s in_ G_, breaking ties arbitrarily. Let_ ball<sub>i</sub>(s) _be the set of vertices strictly closer to s than_ pivot<sub>i</sub>(s)_. Formally,_

\(\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{i}(s)=\{v|\mathrm{s}v|<|\mathrm{spivot}_\mathrm{i}(s)|\}\)

_For each_ \(v\in\mathsf{V}\)_, let_ cluster<sub>i</sub>(v) _be the set of vertices whose ball contains v. Formally,_

\(\mathrm{cluster}_\mathrm{i}(v)=\{s|v\in\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{i}(s)\}\)

We now state the following lemma in \[Gup25\] which bounds the size of balls.

**Lemma 3.4** (\[Gup25\])**.** _For each_ \(0\le\mathrm{i}\le\mathrm{loglog}n-1\) _and each_ \(s\in\mathsf{V}\), \(|\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{i}(s)|=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(2^{2^\mathrm{i}})\) _with a high probability. Moreover, we can compute the following in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2)\) _time with a high probability:_

1. pivot<sub>i</sub>(s) _and its distance from s for all_ \(s\in\mathsf{V}\)_. So,_ est(s,pivot<sub>i</sub>(s))=|spivot<sub>i</sub>(s)|.<tbc>

_2._ ball<sub>i</sub>(s) _for all_ i _and_ \(s\in\mathsf{V}\)_. Moreover,_ est(s,v)=|sv| _for each_ \(v\in\mathrm{ball}_\mathrm{i}(s)\).

The above lemma bounds the number of vertices in ball<sub>i</sub>(s). Furthermore, for each i and s, we can efficiently compute pivot<sub>i</sub>(s) and ball<sub>i</sub>(s). Additionally, we can compute the length of the shortest path from s to each vertex in ball<sub>i</sub>(s).

The above lemma also allows us to compute clusters, but it does not bound their size. The work \[Gup25\] does not use clusters. In contrast, our algorithm uses clusters crucially and requires a bound on the cluster size. However, nested vertex sampling does not guarantee bounded cluster size. To address this issue, we adapt a result of Thorup and Zwick \[TZ01\].

### 3.1 Fast Matrix Multiplication (FMM)

**Definition 3.10** (Distance product or min-plus product)**.** _Let_ A _be a matrix of size_ \(n\times n^r\) _and_ B _be a matrix of size_ \(n^r\times n\)_. The distance product or min-plus product of_ A _and_ B _is defined as_

\((A\star B)_{\mathrm{i}j}:=\mathrm{min}_{1\unknown\ell\unknown n^r}\{A_{\mathrm{i}\ell}+B_{\ell j}\}\)

_where_ \(1\unknown\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}\unknown n\).

The distance product can be computed quickly using fast rectangular matrix multiplication. In our paper, we are satisfied even with an approximate distance product. A matrix C is a \((1+\varepsilon)\) approximation of A ⋆B if, for each i,j,

\((A\star B)_{\mathrm{i}j}\unknown C_{\mathrm{i}j}\unknown(1+\varepsilon)(A\star B)_{\mathrm{i}j}\)

where \(\varepsilon>0\). We use the following result implied in \[Zwi02\], which computes a \((1+\varepsilon)\) approximation of the distance product efficiently. Recently, \[DFK<sup>+</sup>24\] used this result to get better algorithms for additive as well as multiplicative APSP.

**Lemma 3.11** (Implied by \[Zwi02\])**.** _Let_ W _be a positive integer and let_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _be a parameter. Consider matrices_ A _of size_ \(n\times n^r\) _and_ B _of size_ \(n^r\times n\) _where each entry of_ A _and_ B _lies in_ \(\{0,1,\dots,W\}\cup\{\infty\}\)_. Then there exists an algorithm that computes a_ \((1+\varepsilon)\) _approximation of the min-plus product_ A ⋆B _in time_

\(\tilde{\mathrm{O}}\left(\frac{n^{\omega(r)}}{\varepsilon}\mathrm{log}W\right).\)

_Here_ \(\omega(r)\) _is a function that depends on_ r.

In our setting, the maximum finite distance between any two vertices is bounded by O(n). Thus, we can set W=O(n), and the logW factor is absorbed by the \(\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(\cdot)\) notation. Thus, we reduce approximate distance products to rectangular matrix multiplication. In our algorithm, the parameter r is small. Specifically, in our dense case, the inner dimension of the matrix multiplication is n<sup>0.125</sup>, which corresponds to r=0.125. Results in \[Cop82, Wil14\] show that when \(r\unknown 0.17227\) we have \(\omega(r)=2\). Therefore, our algorithm runs in \(\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(n^2)\) time even though it uses FMM.
